chapter_theme: The decade of 'mother' (அன்னாய்ப் பத்து, kurinji, Kapilar): every poem ends on அன்னாய், a girl and her friend speaking of the hill man of secret love, his wilting gift of leaves, his virtue, his coming and going, the omens of his return and the pallor his absence brings, each set against a scene of his hill (211-220).

211.reading: On the hill where the vayalai creeper grows pale as black-gram flour kneaded with ghee, the lovely leaf-skirt of mixed asoka leaves from its top is fading, mother.
211.nuance: The leaf-skirt (தழை) is the lover's gift of secret courtship; that it wilts is all the poem says, and the reader is left to set the withering gift beside a love that is not being renewed. The line has பகைத்தழி, read as பகைத்தழை, a skirt of contrasting leaves.

thinai_evidence.note: the asoka leaf-skirt and the vayalai creeper of the hill

thurai_akam.speaker: thalaivi
thurai_akam.note: speaker inferred: the colophon gives no thurai, only the decade title அன்னாய்ப் பத்து; the poem only reports the leaf-skirt wilting; read as the girl to her friend, the speaker could equally be the friend

212.reading: Why should we be parted from the man of the land where smoke rising from the fragrant wood among the sandal trees smells of blended perfume, a man of virtue, mother?
212.nuance: The girl calls him அறவன், a man of virtue, and that word is the whole of her argument: the fragrance that rises even from the smoke of his land is offered as a sign that nothing ill comes from him.

thinai_evidence.note: the sandal trees and the fragrant wood of the hill

thurai_akam.speaker: thalaivi
thurai_akam.note: speaker inferred: the colophon gives no thurai, only the decade title அன்னாய்ப் பத்து; the first person plural நாம் and the trust in the man suit the girl answering a friend who fears he will leave

213.reading: If the man of the good land high on the slopes comes, where hill people gather the cool big young mangoes that the fragrant mango drops when their stalks break, as one gathers hail fallen with the rain, I can go on living, mother.
213.nuance: The windfall the hill people only have to pick up is set against a life that hangs on his coming. The word பாலையிற் in line 2 is not clear as written and is left unread.

thinai_evidence.note: the mango of the slope and the hill people

thurai_akam.speaker: thalaivi
thurai_akam.note: speaker inferred: the colophon gives no thurai, only the decade title அன்னாய்ப் பத்து; the first person யான் makes the girl the speaker

214.reading: The man of the land where a ripe, fragrant jackfruit from its rich cluster on the slope falls into a cleft of the dark rock and tears open a great honeycomb on the hill goes off to his own fine country, making my wide, cool eyes run with tears, mother.
214.nuance: The fruit does not mean to break the comb; it simply falls, and the honey runs. So the man does no deliberate wrong: he goes back to his own land, and her tears follow from his going as the honey does from the fall.

thinai_evidence.note: the jackfruit and the honeycomb of the rock

thurai_akam.speaker: thalaivi
thurai_akam.note: speaker inferred: the colophon gives no thurai, only the decade title அன்னாய்ப் பத்து; the girl speaks of her own eyes (மழைக்கண்) weeping

ullurai.tenor: the man's going and the girl's tears

pairs.situation: he drops away from her to his own country
her store of sweetness is broken and her eyes run

ullurai.speaker_fit: the girl uses the jackfruit and honeycomb of her own hill slope, things she knows (porul 7.26)

215.reading: In the evening of bush flowers, when the gem-dark bee, black as a touchstone, goes to the narrow-cut ford and hums sweeter than the musicians' flute playing the ambal tune behind the clapper and drum, those who part from us now will do things crueller still, mother.
215.nuance: The evening is not cruel in itself: every sound in it is sweet, the bee sweeter even than the flute. The cruelty is measured by the man who can leave at such an hour, and from that she reasons that he can do worse.

thinai_evidence.note: the millet-field clapper and the bee among bush flowers

thurai_akam.speaker: thalaivi
thurai_akam.note: speaker inferred: the colophon gives no thurai, only the decade title அன்னாய்ப் பத்து; the girl speaks of those who part (பிரிவோர்) as men who leave her

216.reading: Why should your body change, wilting like a plucked shoot, for the man of the land where the strong male of the short-legged great tiger hides in the rich shade of a fruit-laden jackfruit to seize the trembling calf a young she-elephant has borne in the forest of tall bushes, mother?
216.nuance: The friend's question half-answers itself: his land is one where a tiger lies in wait for a newborn calf, so the danger of his road, or of trusting such a man, is in the picture though never said. That reading is not tagged, since no second pair to the situation can be named.

thinai_evidence.note: the tiger, the elephant calf and the jackfruit of the forest

thurai_akam.speaker: thozhi
thurai_akam.note: speaker inferred: the colophon gives no thurai, only the decade title அன்னாய்ப் பத்து; நின் மெய் (your body) makes the friend the speaker, addressing the girl

217.reading: Even though the man of the forest land comes here, where great herds of deer graze on the fragrant gold-like flowers of the vengai on the high hill, why does the body turn pale, mother?
217.nuance: The puzzle is that the pallor comes while he is still coming: secret visits do not cure it. The vengai in flower is the season when marriages were made, which sharpens the question without answering it.

thinai_evidence.note: the vengai of the high hill and the deer herd of the forest

thurai_akam.speaker: thozhi
thurai_akam.note: speaker inferred: the colophon gives no thurai, only the decade title அன்னாய்ப் பத்து; the question about the body here (இவண்) is read as the friend's to the girl

218.reading: My eyes under the fine brows throb and the bangles on my downy forearm grow tight: will the man of the great rocky land come, where a tiger that missed its seizure of a bull elephant rises in fury and roars like rising rain clouds, mother?
218.nuance: Throbbing eyes and bangles that grow tight are good signs, the reverse of the slipping bangles of separation, and she reads them as news of his coming. Yet the land she names is one of a baffled, roaring tiger, so hope and the danger of his road arrive in the same breath.

thinai_evidence.note: the tiger and the bull elephant of the rocky hill

comparisons.tenor: the roar of the angry tiger

thurai_akam.speaker: thalaivi
thurai_akam.note: speaker inferred: the colophon gives no thurai, only the decade title அன்னாய்ப் பத்து; the girl reads signs in her own eyes and bangles

219.reading: Since the man of the good hill went away, where the bright flowers of the black-stemmed vengai with its dark calyx fall and stripe the wide rock, why does that bright forehead turn pale, mother?
219.nuance: The friend asks why, yet states the cause in the same sentence (பிரிந்தென, since he went), so the question is a gentle naming of the grief. The flowers striping the rock recall a tiger's coat, as the tree's name does.

thinai_evidence.note: the vengai and the wide rock of the good hill

thurai_akam.speaker: thozhi
thurai_akam.note: speaker inferred: the colophon gives no thurai, only the decade title அன்னாய்ப் பத்து; ஒண்ணுதல் (the bright forehead) is read as the friend's address to the girl

220.reading: On the days she has not embraced the broad, mighty chest, like a great mountain, of the man of the land where a wide waterfall fed by swaying clouds comes down the slopes of waving bamboo, her cloud-cool eyes, their lids bewildered, run with tears, mother.
220.nuance: Clouds pour the waterfall, and the girl's eyes, called cloud-eyes (மழைக்கண்), pour tears: the hill's water and her weeping are matched by the same word, with no marker joining them.

thinai_evidence.note: the waterfall and bamboo of the hill slope

thurai_akam.speaker: thozhi
thurai_akam.note: speaker inferred: the colophon gives no thurai, only the decade title அன்னாய்ப் பத்து; இவள் (she) speaks of the girl in the third person; read as the friend to the mother, though அன்னாய் may address the friend as elsewhere in the decade

links.note: Ainkurunuru 212: the girl asks why they should be parted from a man of virtue (அறவன்). Kural 1154: the woman asks whether those who trusted the assurances of the one who said 'do not fear' are at fault if he leaves.
links.teaches: The girl rests her whole security on the man's being virtuous, while the Kural imagines that very assurer leaving and moves the blame onto him, so the pair shows that in secret love the only guarantee was his character and the Kural tests it to the point of failure.

links.note: Ainkurunuru 213: the girl says she can live only if he comes. Kural 1263: the wife says she still lives on the longing for her husband's return from war.
links.teaches: For the wife the longing for return is already enough to keep her alive, while the unmarried girl says life itself waits on his coming, so the pair grades the same dependence: hope sustains in marriage, only presence sustains in secret love.

links.note: Ainkurunuru 215: at evening the bee hums sweeter than the musicians' flute, and those who leave then will do worse. Kural 1228: the herdsman's flute is the burning evening's messenger and a killing weapon.
links.teaches: The Kural makes the evening flute itself the weapon, while the Ainkurunuru keeps the music sweet and turns its sweetness into the measure of the leaver's cruelty, so together they show evening music wounding the parted woman not by harshness but by sweetness heard alone.

links.note: Ainkurunuru 217: the friend asks why the girl pales even though the man keeps coming. Kural 1187: the woman says pallor came on her thickly the moment she turned a little in his embrace.
links.teaches: The friend's puzzle, pallor despite his visits, finds its answer in the Kural's hyperbole that the least gap in union breeds pallor, so the pair shows that secret visits, each ending in parting, feed the pallor rather than cure it.

links.note: Ainkurunuru 218: the girl's eyes throb and her bangles tighten, and she asks if he will come. Akananuru 141: answering the anxious friend, the wife says her dreams are sweet and the house birds give good signs, so may he come for the festival.
links.teaches: The Akananuru wife reads hope in dreams and household birds while the Ainkurunuru girl reads it in her own eyes and bangles, so the pair shows the omen-reading of akam reaching from the house to the body, and always voiced by the one who waits, against the friend's fear.

links.note: Ainkurunuru 218: throbbing eyes and tightening bangles promise his coming. Kural 1203: a sneeze that starts and dies away makes the woman fear he began to think of her and stopped.
links.teaches: Both women read the absent man in involuntary signs of their own bodies, but the girl's signs come to completion and promise him while the Kural's sneeze aborts and suggests his forgetting, so the pair shows the same bodily sign-language turned to hope or doubt.

links.note: Ainkurunuru 219: the friend asks why the girl's forehead pales since the hill man went away. Kural 1188: the woman complains that people say she has grown pale, and no one says that he left her.
links.teaches: The friend's question names the man's leaving together with the pallor, which is exactly the acknowledgement the Kural's woman says the world withholds, so the pair shows the friend as the one voice that ties the girl's pallor to the man who caused it.

source_issues: The colophon of every poem in this decade gives thinai (குறிஞ்சி) only, no thurai; speakers are inferred from the poems and recorded in thurai_akam with a note.
211 line 3 பகைத்தழி is read as பகைத்தழை (a skirt of contrasting leaves); the form as printed gives no sense.
213 line 2 பாலையிற் is unclear in context (a paalai tree, or a misreading); the poem's sense does not turn on it.
